title: Resource Development
summary: Resource Development is the tactic covering the infrastructure, identities, and tooling an adversary establishes or acquires before and during a campaign, almost all of which sits on systems the victim does not own and therefore cannot monitor directly. Typical behaviour includes registering lookalike or typosquatted domains, obtaining free or stolen cloud and virtual private server capacity, acquiring code-signing certificates through fraudulent registrations, staging payloads on legitimate file-sharing or code-hosting services, purchasing or renting access from initial-access brokers, and compiling or buying tooling that matches the target's defensive stack. From the defender's side the observable surface is indirect and mostly external: newly registered domains that resemble the brand, certificate transparency entries, DNS resolutions pointing at commodity hosting, mail authentication failures from previously unseen sending infrastructure, and abuse reports from third parties. Threat intelligence platforms, domain monitoring, and collaboration with registrars or hosting providers carry much of the detection weight, while internal telemetry usually only shows the consequences of this preparation, such as phishing sent from aged accounts or payloads downloaded from reputable content networks. The tactic is hard to detect in isolation because none of the preparatory actions are inherently malicious, because infrastructure is often recycled and shared between unrelated customers, and because attribution depends on correlating weak signals over time rather than on any single high-fidelity event.
objectives: Describe the adversary goal behind Resource Development and why most of its activity is invisible to internal monitoring.
Enumerate the observable external artifacts of campaign preparation: new domains, certificates, hosting changes, staged payloads, and broker activity.
Explain how domain and certificate monitoring can be tuned to a specific brand without generating unusable alert volume.
Correlate external infrastructure indicators with inbound email and authentication telemetry to identify a campaign before payload delivery.
Evaluate the limits of attribution when adversaries reuse commodity hosting, compromised legitimate sites, and shared tooling.
Draft an escalation path that turns an external infrastructure observation into a monitored defensive action.
